records.table: Kavalan is Taiwan's single malt house in Yilan County, where subtropical heat and humidity work the spirit and the cask fast. The Kavalan Classic Single Malt Whisky was its first bottling, in 2008: mango, honey and vanilla, gentle enough to pour neat.
records.story: Until Taiwan's entry to the WTO in 2002, alcohol there was a state monopoly and no private company could distil it. The opening came quickly to the King Car Group, a Taiwanese food and drinks company, which built a malt distillery at Yuanshan in Yilan County, completed in 2005. Its first new make ran in March 2006, on 11 March by one account, from copper pot stills of Scottish design. The label takes its name from the Kavalan, the Indigenous people of the Yilan plain, whose name was long the old name of the county itself. The first bottling, the Classic, went on sale in December 2008, less than three years after the first spirit. By the house's own account the subtropical heat and humidity of Yilan quicken the exchange between spirit and oak, which is how so young a malt shows ripe fruit and a full colour. For a bartender the Classic is the bottle that teaches the point the Cask Atlas makes: climate changes the pace of maturation, but a year in Yilan is one year, and no number of Scottish years is in the glass.

records.table: Amrut is India's single malt house from the edge of Bengaluru, and Amrut Fusion joins Indian barley with peated barley from Scotland. Bottled strong, it gives citrus, dark chocolate and a gentle smoke, and a few drops of water open it.
records.story: Amrut began in Bangalore in 1948, the year after Indian independence, and grew as a maker of spirits for the Indian market. Its malt distillery at Kambipura, on the Mysore Road outside the city, was built in 1987. Its malt went first into the company's blended whiskies for the Indian market, until it chose to bottle a single malt and take it abroad. The launch came in Glasgow, at Cafe India, on 24 August 2004: an Indian single malt offered first in Scotland. The founder's son led the company through those years until his death in 2019. Fusion followed in 2009, named for its recipe: Indian barley and peated barley from Scotland, distilled and matured apart in American oak and then married. The distillery stands about 3,000 feet above sea level, and by its own account the heat there speeds the work between spirit and wood. For a bartender Fusion is the plain lesson that a malt from a warm country can be young and yet deep, and that peat need not come from an island.

records.table: Starward is Melbourne's single malt house, and Starward Nova spends its whole life in Australian red wine barrels, filled while wet with wine. It pours red berries, toasted oak and cinnamon spice, and it makes a bright highball.
records.story: Starward began in 2007, when its founder turned an old Qantas maintenance hangar at Essendon Fields, beside Melbourne's Essendon Airport, into a distillery. From the start the house set out to make a whisky of its own city, using barley grown close by and barrels from Australian wineries. Its first release, Solera, came in 2013, matured in casks that had held apera, the Australian name for a sherry style wine. Spirit was also filled into red wine barrels, mainly shiraz and cabernet from the Barossa and Yarra valleys, for a release first called Wine Cask and later renamed Nova. In 2016 the distillery moved to a larger warehouse in Port Melbourne. The house credits Melbourne's swings of temperature with quickening the work between spirit and oak. For a bartender Nova teaches the wine cask as a house style rather than a finish: the red fruit comes from barrels the whisky never leaves, and it shows a guest that Australian whisky is not only Tasmanian.

records.table: Sullivans Cove is the Tasmanian single malt house of Cambridge, outside Hobart, and Sullivans Cove French Oak Single Cask is one French oak cask that held Australian tawny. Expect dark fruit, plum jam and caramel, and a strength and age that change from cask to cask.
records.story: Tasmania banned distilling in 1838, and the island made no whisky for more than a century and a half, until the law was changed in the early 1990s. Tasmania Distillery was founded in 1994 on Hobart's waterfront at Sullivans Cove, the old harbour that gave the whisky its name. By the house's account its first spirit ran in March 1995, and that spirit was bottled as its first single malt in March 1997. The business changed hands more than once in its early years, and in 2004 the distillery moved from the waterfront to a small warehouse at Cambridge, outside Hobart. There the house kept its habit: Tasmanian barley, slow distillation in copper, and each release drawn from one cask, numbered, and bottled unfiltered. Its French oak casks that once held Australian tawny became the bottling a guest asks for by name. For a bartender the bottle carries two lessons: Tasmania is told apart from the mainland, and a single cask is a release, never a recipe, so the strength and the age are read off the bottle in hand.

bottle.name: Penderyn Madeira Finish
bottle.class: Single Malt Welsh Whisky, a protected geographical indication since 2023
bottle.mash: Malted barley only, brewed into a wash on site in the distillery's own mash tun.
bottle.still: Distilled at Penderyn, where the Faraday still, a single copper still designed for the distillery, draws spirit at 92 per cent alcohol in one distillation; a second Faraday still followed in 2013 and two copper pot stills in 2014.

records.table: Penderyn is the Welsh single malt from the village of Penderyn, at the edge of the Brecon Beacons, and Penderyn Madeira Finish is its house style: bourbon barrels, then casks that held Madeira. It gives cream toffee, raisins and tropical fruit.
records.story: Whisky had not been distilled in Wales for more than a century when, as the house tells it, a small group of friends talking in a pub in the shadow of the Brecon Beacons resolved to change that. The Welsh Whisky Company was founded in 1998, and on 14 September 2000 the first spirit ran at Penderyn, a village chosen in part for its spring water by one account, from a single still of new design, the Faraday still. The whisky consultant Jim Swan (died 2017), an adviser from its early years, judged, by the house's account, that the spirit should be finished in Madeira casks, and the Madeira finish became the house style. The first single malt, sold by one account as Aur Cymru, Welsh gold, went on sale on St David's Day, 1 March 2004, a Madeira finish bottled without chill filtering. The distillery grew in 2013 and 2014, when a second Faraday still and then two copper pot stills were installed, and the house opened two more distilleries, at Llandudno in 2021 and in Swansea in 2023. In July 2023 Single Malt Welsh Whisky became a protected geographical indication. For a bartender the Madeira Finish is the bottle that says Wales: a light, fruity malt, and the cask the house has kept since its first release.
